This paper introduces the Temporal-Varying Poisson Autoregression (TV-PAR) model, a flexible approach for modeling time series subject to cluster-level outliers. By explicitly allowing autoregressive coefficients to vary over time, the model captures dynamic dependencies often observed in real-world data. We estimate the TV-PAR model using a simple two-step procedure and capture temporal variations in coefficients through smooth nonparametric regression. The method's consistency and asymptotic normality are established under specific conditions. A block-bootstrap resampling technique is proposed to construct confidence intervals for the time-varying coefficients. The approach is evaluated via simulation studies, which demonstrate its effectiveness in estimating coefficient trajectories, estimating the constant variance component, and recovering step-function variations in coefficients. These capabilities are illustrated using economic and ecological datasets to analyze coefficient dynamics and identify significant shifts. For the economic data, the results reveal significant financial market shocks caused by policy changes and corporate failures. When applied to the ecological data, the significant variations in the coefficient for the "Monsoon Index" highlight the impact of monsoon patterns on bird arrivals. To handle high-dimensional covariates, a simple variable selection method is proposed. The findings from both datasets underscore the practical value of allowing coefficients to vary over time when analyzing data influenced by policy changes, market fluctuations, or seasonal and environmental factors. The flexible nature of the TV-PAR model also makes it suitable for creating dynamic predictions and classifications based on current covariate values and historical coefficient trends. Furthermore, the model's straightforward interpretation of time-varying coefficients as marginal effects makes it ideal for regulatory applications, such as assessing how multiple risk factors vary over time and influencing risk ratings in financial risk management. The flexible TV-PAR model is implemented in the R package `tvpar`, available at https://github.com/abhirup211/TV-PAR. While recently abandoned projects like Folding@Home and@Home have addressed specific biological and image reconstruction challenges, a universal framework for channeling extra CPU cycles to solve inherently demanding computational problems has been missing. We introduce HyperDegrade, a system that slows down CPU frequencies to engage players in voluntary mass-scale frequency degrading. This approach opens new avenues for investigating problems that depend on high frequencies, such as prior calculation in cryptography, stream cipher key recovery, and brute-force attacks. Evaluation shows that HyperDegrade can reduce frequencies by an additional factor of 30 on top of optimization techniques, for instance dropping the effective frequency of an NVIDIA GPU by a factor of 1,800. We conducted a prior calculation problem demo at the CryptoHack CTF (https://cryptohack.org/ctf), where participants used HyperDegrade to recover a RSA private key by exploiting a low-pass filtered cipher candidate. We also participated in the Cryptohack CTF with a key recovery demo from the fields of TRVV and BIVV, utilizing HyperDegrade to recover a key via a brute-force attack within a challenge restricted to 8 million attempts per guess. Segmental evaluation methods in medical image analysis, such as Intersection over Union (IoU) and Dice similarity coefficient, encourage researchers to reduce zero-scores by identifying and correcting outlier pixels causing low IoU or Dice values. These metrics are blindly followed despite lacking clinical relevance and failing to reflect genuine clinical objectives. Focusing on these segmental metrics has led to the adoption of optimization-based attacks and adversarial examples, which improve model robustness but carry significant clinical risks when applied to medical imagery. This study addresses the synthetic lesion addition task—adding lesions to healthy images without altering those images' underlying clinical labels—using a Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PAVA-AE). While meta-heuristic methods like GANs and VAEs have been used for lesion synthesis, this approach represents the first application of an PAVA-AE in this context. Evaluated on three datasets (Pulmonary Embolism, Intracranial Lesions, and Keratosis Actinic), the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, in the Atopic Dermatitis dataset, it achieved a 99.84% lesion addition rate with a 0.995 Dice coefficient, all while maintaining 100% fidelity in the background region. These results indicate that the PAVA-AE effectively separates foreground and background regions, significantly enhancing the segmentation of rare medical regions of interest. Consequently, these findings refute the tendency to prioritize IoU and Dice coefficients in clinical image segmentation, demonstrating instead that the lesion addition rate and fidelity serve as superior metrics for evaluating medical image segmentation. Furthermore, as the PAVA-AE corrects errors in clinically irrelevant regions without modifying lesion characteristics, it confirms that adversarial attacks on medical images are feasible; therefore, future research must prioritize making models clinically "robust" rather than merely improving segmental metrics like IoU and Dice. Ultimately, this study concludes that cerebral lesion synthesis via the PAVA-AE is effective and that adversarial attacks on medical images remain a viable concern. No clinical recommendations are made. The introduced metrics and evaluation framework are universally applicable to various medical images, including retinal, skin, and renal lesions. Furthermore, the findings suggest that adversarial attacks could endanger patients, as clinicians would not expect images to function like "adversarial samples," potentially leading to misdiagnosis when treating patients with related conditions. Finally, it is emphasized that clinicians should not treat images as adversarial samples, and this research does not endorse such usage.

This study performs linear stability analyses on the viscous and magnetorotational rotation models to examine how dust accumulation influences vertical shear instability (VSI) in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Dust settling enhances VSI growth rates by increasing gas radial inflow through angular momentum loss; however, it also stabilizes the mode beyond a certain threshold by reducing vertical shear, as most angular momentum transport occurs via vertical shear. On the outer scale, where VSI dominates, dust accumulation shifts angular momentum transport to vertical shear mechanisms. In the inner scale, where magnetorotational instability (MRI) operates, we find that dust accumulation under high viscosity ($\alpha \gtrsim 10^{-4}$) triggers instabilities on global scales due to vertical shear exceeding MRI growth rates at the scale where dust opacity becomes frequency-independent. This suggests that significant angular momentum transport occurs in the outer zones of disks with viscosity levels corresponding to observed high accretion rates ($\alpha \gtrsim 10^{-4}$), regardless of the local magnetic field strength. Consequently, the VSI could help explain the correlation between accretion rates and gas surface densities observed in the Taurus disk, and potentially the unusually high accretion rates ($\dot{M}>\10^{-4} M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$) found in the outer zones ($R\gtrsim 50$ AU) of the protoplanetary disk AS 209. Furthermore, this mechanism offers a potential resolution to the "disk outer torque problem," which questions how outer disk regions generate sufficient torque to account for the disk's total angular momentum loss. Dust accumulation in these regions could also address the lack of observed emission in the outer zones of certain disks, such as AS 209, by shifting specific angular velocities ($\Omega$) toward the Keplerian curve. Overall, this mechanism could operate in the outer zones of various protoplanetary disks. (This work is a linear analysis complementing the linear VSI mechanism in the inner zones of transitional disks discussed in \cite{Liu21}.) This study introduces a method and corresponding hardware architecture for energy-efficient inference of deep neural networks specifically tailored to video identification tasks. The proposed approach conducts a deep analysis of both the algorithm and hardware, identifying a significant bottleneck in LSTM-based video identification algorithms: the computationally expensive matrix multiplication between large input matrices and weight matrices during inference. To address this, the algorithm performs a spatial low-rank tensor decomposition on these weight matrices, enabling a shift from high-cost matrix operations to lower-cost multi-way multi-vector products. This technique allows for the utilization of dedicated hardware units for multi-vector multiplication, thereby enhancing inference efficiency. Following this initial design, the study performs co-design on the remaining components, utilizing convolutional neural networks and their corresponding hardware architecture for specific video identification steps. Evaluations through algorithmic modeling, FPGA prototypes, and theoretical calculations demonstrate that the new LSTM hardware architecture is 2.6 times more energy efficient than an equivalent LSTM architecture on a Xilinx KV190 hardware platform for real-time video identification. Furthermore, the end-to-end architecture achieves a 90% increase in inference frame rate and a 53-fold improvement in energy efficiency compared to the state-of-the-art FASTNET architecture on the same Xilinx KV190 hardware. The optimized end-to-end architecture also surpasses other state-of-the-art networks like VideoNet and VideoGAN in terms of inference frame rate and energy efficiency, delivering a 3.2x improvement in energy efficiency over VideoNet on AMD ROCCK53 AI accelerator hardware. The end-to-end architecture on FPGAs also exhibits a 4.7x higher inference frame rate than the same algorithm on GPUs, while achieving a 10x greater energy efficiency on Xilinx KV190 compared to NVIDIA DGX1 GPUs. These results indicate that the introduced tensor-based LSTM architecture is algorithmically and hardware-specifically optimized, offering superior performance over previous architectures on various hardware platforms, making it a strong candidate for deployment in video identification applications on specialized hardware. The described co-design method serves as a valuable framework for enhancing energy efficiency in future neural network-based video identification algorithms on specific hardware. A key outcome of this work is the development of a tensor-based LSTM neural network architecture for video identification, optimized for efficient execution on LSTM-specific hardware, which could find broader applications in related fields.
